transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-08-10 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48m
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maya Reed (Redwood CSM), Marcus Varela (Halosys CTO), Lena Ortiz (ML Eng), Tony Wu (Procurement)
Shared links: deck (https://redwood.ai/decks/halosys-aug10), bench CSV (https://redwood.ai/bench/halosys-aug10.csv), security brief (drive/halosys/soc2-appendix.pdf)

Summary: Quick readout of latest lab bench vs baseline provider. Focus areas: tail latency, throughput under mixed payloads, routing fallback, quantization tradeoffs, next steps for dedicated capacity ask. Noise: some crosstalk and a few transcription errors (KV cash appears in record).

00:00 Jordan Lee: okay hey everyone thanks for joining on time, um this is our weekly lab readout for the HalOsys POC, we want to go over the consolidated numbers we pulled this week, then priya will talk tuning notes and then open for questions.
01:02 Marcus Varela: awesome, thanks Jordan, quick note on time zones, i gotta hop at 16:45 if we can do procurement last that would be great.
01:17 Jordan Lee: yep noted, we'll do the ask items before procurement. Priya, take it away on the numbers.
01:30 Priya Nair: cool, um so we ran three workload profiles this sprint, short chat (256 tokens), mid (1k tokens) and long form (4k tokens), also mixed concurrency at 8, 32, and 128 to simulate burst; CSV is linked. Baseline is IncumbentProviderX running model variant IP-13; our runs used rwx-1.2 quantized int8 and a fallback rwx-1.2 fp16 for cold starts.
02:12 Priya Nair: headline: median latency for short chat was 38ms vs baseline 44ms, so about 14% improvement; p95 for mid-length was 220ms vs baseline 185ms — so we saw a p95 regression there, mainly under concurrent 128 load when caching didn't hit.
02:45 Lena Ortiz: wait — p95 regression on mid length, is that with quantization enabled?
02:52 Priya Nair: yeah with int8 quant on primary route. we saw some dequantization overhead plus extra kernel schedule delays when sequence lengths vary a lot, that's the main suspect.
03:10 Jordan Lee: to clarify, the throughput numbers?
03:16 Priya Nair: throughput: for long-form steady-state we hit 62 tokens/sec per GPU on our profile vs baseline 51 tokens/sec, so ~21% throughput win; however tail latency under burst handling (128 concurrent) spikes to 1.2s p99 vs baseline 750ms.
03:45 Marcus Varela: hmm that p99 spike is our primary worry, users care about tail for interactive editing flows.
03:52 Maya Reed: understood, and this is where routing/fallback helps, we can route to fp16 variant for those tails.
04:10 Tony Wu: cost question, if we route to fp16 more often how does that change unit cost?
04:18 Priya Nair: rough estimate in this lab: fp16 route is ~23% more cost per token but reduces p99 by 45% in these bursts. We'll include more granular token-level cost in the spreadsheet.
05:00 Marcus Varela: do you have the exact traffic mix we used? our production is ~70% short, 25% mid, 5% long but with occasional spikes to long when batch jobs run.
05:15 Priya Nair: we used a 60/30/10 split to stress mid and long a bit more; if you can share your 70/25/5 we'll re-run with that mix.
05:30 Lena Ortiz: yes i'll drop the live mix into the shared folder by EOD.
06:02 Priya Nair: cool. A couple of anomalies: we saw KV cash misses — uh KV cache misses — on the first 12 minutes after a routing config change, that inflated p95 for mid. There's also an optimizer thread contention at the kernel selection layer under mixed sequence lengths. We have a patch to prefer homogenous kernel scheduling which reduced p95 by ~18% in a local re-run.
07:00 Jordan Lee: can you explain the homogenous kernel pref patch in plain English for the infra folks?
07:10 Priya Nair: sure, basically when requests of very different seq lengths hit the same worker the runtime picks different kernels and has to context-switch, causing scheduling stalls. The patch biases requests with adjacent seq length to the same kernel lane or pins short sequences to a fast path, less context switches. Implementation is config toggle, low risk.
07:55 Marcus Varela: sounds promising. any security or compliance impact?
08:00 Maya Reed: none, it's infra tuning only. We won't change data handling or logging. Security docs remain the same.
08:20 Tony Wu: procurement question — if we need dedicated slots during spikes, what's minimum commitment and SLA?
08:28 Jordan Lee: standard Dedicated proposal is monthly reserved slots with burst buffer; minimum purchase for enterprise pilot is 2x GPU slots for a month, with optional hourly burst. SLA for latency is tiered, we can share an excerpt.
08:45 Tony Wu: please share pricing; our finance team will want monthly vs annual numbers.
08:50 Jordan Lee: will do, action on me to share pricing grid.
09:15 Priya Nair: back to bench — routing playbook: default route is quantized int8, fallback to fp16 at 300ms tail threshold, with optional canary to dedicated pool when qps crosses 80% of target. We tested threshold at 300ms and 500ms; 300ms keeps cost low but increases observed p99; 500ms reduces p99 but increases fp16 usage ~12%.
10:05 Marcus Varela: what's the recommended threshold for our mix?
10:12 Priya Nair: with your 70/25/5 mix I'd recommend 350ms as a compromise, but we'll re-run to confirm.
10:30 Marcus Varela: ok.
11:05 Lena Ortiz: on quantization — we saw a small delta in output probabilities for some classification edge cases, any QA notes?
11:12 Priya Nair: yep a few top-k re-ranks differ by 0.2-0.5% for rare tokens, we surfaced these in the eval harness. We can pin precision-sensitive routes to fp16.
11:35 Lena Ortiz: good, we'll identify two customer-critical routes to keep fp16.
12:00 Jordan Lee: quick note about benchmark alignment, some labels in the CSV refer to IP-13 as "InciProvider" due to transcription import errors, ignore those typos.
12:25 Marcus Varela: ha noted. any infrastructure requests from your side?
12:32 Priya Nair: we requested a short-lived SSH into your test VPC for an egress check, but that depends on your security team. Alternatively we can run a synthetic from our dedicated VPC that mirrors your CIDR for latency approximations.
12:50 Marcus Varela: security will prefer no inbound, so the synthetic mirror approach sounds better.
13:10 Maya Reed: we'll set up the mirror and share the config.
13:30 Tony Wu: procurement timeline — we are targeting a decision by end of month (8/31). Are there blockers to making a recommendation by then?
13:40 Jordan Lee: no blockers besides the dedicated-slot pricing approval and one more bench run with your traffic mix. If we get your traffic file by 8/12 we can deliver updated numbers by 8/13 and a recommended routing/playbook.
14:05 Lena Ortiz: i'll upload the traffic file today.
14:30 Priya Nair: another datapoint: when we turned on prefix caching for chat flows, token cost fell by 9% and p50 improved by ~10ms, but cold start p95 was unaffected. So caching helps steady-state but doesn't solve the burst tail spikes.
15:00 Marcus Varela: okay that fits our observations.
15:20 Jordan Lee: quick question to Marcus — for the decision criteria, beyond latency/p99 and cost, what are the must-haves?
15:30 Marcus Varela: must-haves: SOC2 compliance, KMS integration, audit logs retention 12+ months, and a vendor that supports private VPC deployment in our region.
15:45 Maya Reed: we have SOC2 and KMS notes in that security brief link, and Redwood Private supports VPC in the region (we'll attach the region-specific note). Audit logs retention is configurable, we'll include retention SLAs.
16:10 Tony Wu: great, please share those.
16:25 Priya Nair: one more thing — in a head-to-head with IncumbentProviderX we run a 10-minute rolling spike test, Redwood averaged 18% fewer token compute ops but had 28% higher p99 in the worst-case. That suggests different resource scheduling assumptions; the fix is route tuning + kernel bias patch and possibly dedicated slots.
17:05 Marcus Varela: so summary: wins on median and throughput, regression on tail under huge bursts. we either accept the higher tail via cost tradeoffs or we use routing + dedicated pool.
17:18 Jordan Lee: exactly. If you're comfortable, our recommended next steps are: we run one additional bench with your real traffic (Lena to share), Priya to enable homogenous kernel pref and run tail-specific tests, Jordan to send a Dedicated pricing worksheet, and Maya to share SOC2/KMS/region notes.
17:45 Marcus Varela: yes that sounds like the path.
18:00 Tony Wu: last procurement note — if dedicated slots are needed, can we start with a 30-day pilot and then escalate?
18:08 Jordan Lee: yes, we can structure a 30-day reserved pilot with an opt-in extension, we'll draft terms.
18:25 Marcus Varela: ok i have to jump now, thanks, Lena will follow up on the traffic file.
18:35 Jordan Lee: thanks Marcus. Lena, Tony, any other questions before we wrap?
18:42 Lena Ortiz: no, i'll drop files and flag the two precision-sensitive routes.
18:50 Tony Wu: nothing else.
18:55 Maya Reed: recap: next steps and action items noted, you'll get the pricing and security docs by Friday; bench re-run by Priya on 8/13, Jordan will upload benchmark CSV edit and playbook.
19:10 Jordan Lee: perfect, thanks everyone. meeting adjourned.

Notes on transcript quality: some words garbled (e.g., KV cash), occasional speaker mislabels, timestamps approximate.
